question: An undirected graph has 12 vertices, 4 connected components and 9 edges. What can you conclude?
option_a: It has a cycle: a forest with 4 components on 12 vertices has 8 edges
option_b: It is a forest, because 9 edges is fewer than the 12 vertices it has
option_c: It is a single tree, because a tree on 12 vertices needs exactly 11 edges
option_d: Nothing, because edge counts alone never reveal whether a cycle exists
explanation: A forest with c components on n vertices has exactly n − c edges, here 8. Any edge beyond that joins two vertices that are already connected, which creates a cycle.

question: This code is meant to detect a directed cycle. What is wrong with it?
option_a: It recurses, so it is wrong even on small graphs that it could easily handle
option_b: It never marks vertices, so it loops forever on any graph containing a cycle
option_c: It reports a cycle for a diamond 0→1, 0→2, 1→2, which has no directed cycle at all
option_d: It misses self-loops, because seen[u] is set only after the loop over adj[u]
explanation: Being visited is not the same as being on the current path. Vertex 2 is finished when 0 reaches it again, so it must count as black (safe). The fix is three colours: report a cycle only when v is grey.

question: In an undirected DFS, why must the edge back to the parent be skipped?
option_a: Because the parent is always black, and black vertices never take part in a cycle
option_b: Because it is the tree edge just used to arrive, not a second route
option_c: Because skipping it halves the running time of the DFS on dense graphs
option_d: Because without skipping it the DFS would revisit the parent and loop forever
explanation: An undirected edge appears in both endpoint lists. When u looks at its parent, it is looking at the same edge it arrived by, not a new path. Skip it by edge id, so that a genuine parallel edge is still reported as a 2-cycle.

question: Union-find processes these undirected edges in order. What does it report?
code:
n = 5, edges: 0-1, 2-3, 1-2, 4-4, 3-0
// report the 0-based index of the first edge whose endpoints already share a root
option_a: 4, the edge 3-0, because it is the first edge between two already connected vertices
option_b: 2, the edge 1-2, because it connects the two components that existed before it
option_c: -1, because the graph as a whole is a single connected tree with five edges
option_d: 3, the edge 4-4, because a self-loop has both endpoints in the same set already
explanation: After 0-1, 2-3 and 1-2 the set is {0,1,2,3} and {4}. The self-loop 4-4 has find(4) == find(4), so it closes a cycle first, before 3-0 (index 4) does.

question: Which statement characterises bipartite graphs exactly?
option_a: A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no cycle of odd length
option_b: A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no cycle of any length at all
option_c: A graph is bipartite if and only if every vertex has an even degree
option_d: A graph is bipartite if and only if it is connected and has an even number of vertices
explanation: Colours must alternate around every cycle, which only works for even lengths, and the BFS colouring argument shows that a graph without odd cycles can always be two-coloured. Even cycles (a square) are fine, so B is too strong.

question: During a BFS colouring by depth parity, edge u–v joins two vertices of the same colour. Why must depth[u] equal depth[v]?
option_a: Because BFS assigns every vertex in a component the same depth before moving on
option_b: Because BFS edges join depths differing by at most 1, and 1 flips the parity
option_c: Because u and v were discovered by the same parent, which forces them into one layer
option_d: Because the conflict is always detected on a self-loop, where both ends are one vertex
explanation: If an edge joined depths d and d + 2, the deeper vertex would have been discovered from the shallower one at depth d + 1. So depths differ by 0 or 1, and equal parity forces 0. Walking both ends up to their LCA then gives an odd cycle of length 2k + 1.

question: A vertex in a directed graph is "safe" when every walk from it ends at a vertex without outgoing edges. Which vertices are unsafe?
option_a: Exactly the vertices that lie on a directed cycle, and no others
option_b: Exactly the vertices with in-degree 0, since nothing can reach them
option_c: Exactly the vertices that can reach a directed cycle, including those on one
option_d: Exactly the vertices whose out-degree is larger than their in-degree
explanation: A walk that never stops must repeat a vertex, so it enters a cycle. A vertex that can reach a cycle has such a walk even if it is not on the cycle itself. Peeling from the terminals over the reverse graph finds the safe ones.

question: In parity union-find, root ru has parity pu for u and root rv has parity pv for v. The new constraint is t (0 = same team, 1 = different). Which link is correct?
option_a: par[rv] = t, since the two roots themselves are the vertices being constrained
option_b: par[rv] = pu ^ pv, since t is already implied by the parities of u and v
option_c: par[rv] = pu ^ t, since only the side that keeps its root needs adjusting
option_d: par[rv] = pu ^ pv ^ t, so v's new parity differs from u's by t
explanation: After linking, parity'(v) = pv ^ par[rv]. We need pu ^ parity'(v) == t, so par[rv] = pu ^ pv ^ t. Setting it to t would only be right when u and v are themselves the roots.

question: What is the time complexity of finding the girth (shortest cycle) of an undirected graph by running a BFS from every vertex?
option_a: O(n + m), because each BFS stops as soon as it meets the first non-tree edge
option_b: O(n·(n + m)), because there are n breadth-first searches of O(n + m) each
option_c: O(m log n), because the shortest cycle can be found with a priority queue
option_d: O(n³), because the BFS must be replaced by Floyd-Warshall on cyclic graphs
explanation: One BFS is not enough: the first non-tree edge it meets only gives an upper bound unless the root lies on a shortest cycle. Running it from every root costs n times O(n + m); pruning helps in practice but not in the worst case.

question: Processes P and Q each hold one printer and each wait for one more. The system has 3 printers and process R holds the third, waiting for nothing. Is there a deadlock?
option_a: Yes, because P waits for Q and Q waits for P, which forms a cycle in the wait-for graph
option_b: Yes, because every printer is allocated and no process can be granted anything now
option_c: No, because R can finish and release its printer, which lets P finish and then Q
option_d: No, because a deadlock needs at least three processes to form a waiting cycle
explanation: With several instances per resource, a cycle in the wait-for graph does not imply deadlock. Graph reduction finishes R (request fits), adds its printer to the pool, then P and Q can finish in turn. Only processes left after reduction are deadlocked.

question: The iterative three-colour DFS starts at vertex 0 and scans neighbours in the listed order. Which cycle does it return?
code:
edges: 0→1, 1→2, 2→0, 1→3, 3→1
// on a grey hit u→v it returns v … u by walking parent pointers from u up to v
option_d: 1 2 0 3, the union of the two cycles through vertex 1
explanation: From 0 the DFS goes 0→1→2. Vertex 2 examines 2→0 while 0 is grey, so it returns parent walk 2, 1, then 0, reversed to 0 1 2. The edge 1→3 is never examined, because the search stops at the first back edge.
